title: True riches
hookLine: the one who has little and wants nothing more is rich (Letters 110)

lines: A PARADE OF SILVER AND GOLD.
cards: A parade is coming down a street in Rome. Not soldiers. Wealth.
Wagons of silver plate, gold cups, fabrics in colors most people will never wear, carried past the crowd so everyone can see what a great house owns.
Attalus, the Stoic teacher from two days ago, stands in that crowd and feels the pull of it. In Letter 110, Seneca says Attalus used to tell this story on himself.
What interests Seneca is what Attalus said to himself while the wagons were still rolling by.

teach.b: First, displayed, not owned. Attalus asked himself: what are you staring at? This is a show.
These things are carried past to be looked at, and in a few hours the street will be empty. Even their owners mostly own them the way you own a parade: briefly, at a distance, with worry.
Second, what nature asks for. Seneca turns the story into a short sermon of his own. The body's real needs are small: bread when hungry, water when thirsty.
Nobody, he says, is poor in those.

teach.h: LITTLE, AND WANTING NO MORE, IS RICH.
teach.b: The rest is built by wanting, and wanting has no top floor. Third, the rich person, redefined.

teach.h: ENOUGH IS A NUMBER YOU CHOOSE.
teach.b: Whoever keeps their desires inside what they actually need, Seneca says, can compete with the gods themselves for happiness. That's his wild claim: the person with little who wants nothing more isn't scraping by.
They're rich, in the only way that can't be taken in a single night. Back on day four hundred thirty-four, Letter 2 said the poor person is the one who craves more. Letter 110 says the other half.

Fourth, a fair word. Seneca wrote this as a very wealthy man, and in a few days we'll look at that gap honestly. For now, take the idea on its own: enough is a number you choose, not one the parade chooses for you.

how: Readers of Seneca sometimes write down what 'enough' looks like in one part of their life, and return to it when they feel the pull to want more.

o: a fortune shared out among all your friends
a fortune locked away for a rainy day
having little and wanting nothing more

s: Attalus never felt the pull of wealth himself
Seneca says Attalus told the story of feeling it at a parade of riches.
Seneca says no one is poor in what nature actually needs
bread and water: the rest is built by wanting.
Seneca wrote this as a poor man
he was very wealthy, a gap the path looks at in a few days.

games.q: you're in the crowd as wagons of silver roll past and you feel the wanting. what does Attalus say to himself?
o: what are you staring at? it's a show, and it'll pass.
the people who own this must be happy.
games.why: he reminds himself it's displayed, not owned, and in a few hours the street will be empty.

practice: Take one corner of your life, food, clothes, your phone, your evenings, and ask what would genuinely be enough there: not ideal, enough.
Name it plainly, then notice whether you already have it, and if you don't, whether the gap is smaller than the parade made it seem.

wordCard.voice: True riches. In Letter 110: having little and wanting nothing more. The parade is displayed, not owned. Enough is yours. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'enough': the word under Seneca's idea of true riches.

carryVoice: Your line: rich in enough. Wanting has no top floor, but enough does. Until tomorrow.
